title: AP CSP — Lesson 17 Homework: Lists & Abstraction
notice: All questions are original. Q1–Q6 are AP-style practice, not official AP questions. Q7–Q12 and all marks are teacher-designed. Q5 earns one mark only for both correct choices and no others. Q5: select exactly TWO. AP list indices start at 1. Indexed operations use 1 through current LENGTH; invalid indices cause an error. All examples use simple lists.

questions.prompt: After a ← 4; b ← a; a ← 9, what is b?
questions.explanation: A copies the earlier value 4. B treats assignment as a live link. C invents addition. D invents a reset.
B is the second element. A uses the first position; C the third; D confuses index with value.

questions.prompt: Starting with a ← [12, 7, 20], execute a[2] ← 9. What is a?
questions.explanation: C replaces position 2. A inserts; B updates position 1; D appends. Update preserves length.

questions.prompt: After a ← [8, 5]; REMOVE(a, 1), which access is valid?
questions.explanation: D accesses the sole remaining value 5. The new length is 1; indices 0, 2, 5 are invalid.

questions.prompt: Which TWO statements are true? Select exactly TWO answers.

options.label: D
options.text: A list cannot contain duplicate values.

questions.explanation: A counts zero elements. C adds one element at the end. B mistakes an index for a searched value. D contradicts ordered lists, which may contain duplicates.

questions.prompt: Why can a list of session minutes manage program complexity?

options.label: B
options.text: One named collection can hold changing numbers of related entries.

options.label: C
options.text: It guarantees every entry is correct.

options.label: D
options.text: It removes the need to check indices.

questions.explanation: B identifies a concrete abstraction benefit. Lists do not guarantee speed, data correctness or valid indices, so A,C,D are unsupported.

questions.prompt: For a ← [5, 5, 12, 8], give (a) a[1], (b) a[3], (c) LENGTH(a) , and (d) all valid indices.

Start with a ← [10, 20, 30]. Give the full list after each step in order:
(a) APPEND(a, 40)
(b) INSERT(a, 2, 15)
(c) REMOVE(a, 4)
(d) a[1] ← 5

rubric.criterion: Correct list after INSERT, shifting old indices 2 onward right.
Correct list after removing current index 4.
Correct list after replacement at index 1.

questions.prompt: Each case starts independently with a ← [4, 8, 12]. Give the final list after (a) a[2] ← 6, (b) INSERT(a, 2, 6), (c) APPEND(a, 6), and (d) REMOVE(a, 2).
Write four statements: (a) create sessions as [15, 30]; (b) append 45; (c) change the first value to 20; (d) display the current last element using LENGTH.

rubric.criterion: Displays the element at current LENGTH, not a hard-coded last index.

questions.prompt: Trace separately: a ← []; APPEND(a, 30). Give (a) final a, (b) LENGTH(a) , (c) a[1], and (d) what happens if a[0] is then accessed.

rubric.criterion: Index 0 causes an error and program termination.

questions.prompt: A program stores session minutes in separate variables s1,s2,s3. (a) Propose a meaningful list name. (b) Give a list literal for 10, 20, 30. (c) Explain how an extra session can be added without inventing s4. (d) State one requirement that a list alone does not guarantee.
questions.answer: (a) sessions. (b) [10, 20, 30]. (c) APPEND(sessions,newValue) adds an entry to the collection. (d) For example, entries must still be checked for valid minute values; a list does not guarantee correctness.
questions.explanation: (a) sessions. (b) [10, 20, 30]. (c) APPEND(sessions,newValue) adds an entry to the collection. (d) For example, entries must still be checked for valid minute values; a list does not guarantee correctness.

rubric.criterion: Explains APPEND or equivalent collection operation avoids another separate variable.
Identifies a genuine remaining requirement, such as valid data or valid indices, without claiming guaranteed speed.
